cur:catacombs-louvre-teaching-ma2958.summary: Christ sits enthroned at the centre, raising his hand as he teaches, while the apostles sit on either side in two animated rows, scrolls in hand, turning towards him. The composition, taken from images of philosophers and their pupils, proclaims Christ as the one true Teacher.
facts: Commons records that it was found at Rignieux-le-Franc (Ain), in eastern France.
The Louvre's photographer describes the main face as 'Christ enthroned at the centre teaching the apostles'.

cur:catacombs-ravenna-rinaldo-sarcophagu.summary: Between palm trees, Christ is seated at the centre holding a book, while Peter and Paul bow towards him from either side, offering wreaths. The scaly, rounded lid is typical of Ravenna. Carved in the 5th century, the sarcophagus was later reused for the 14th-century archbishop Rinaldo da Concorreggio.
facts: Commons dates the sarcophagus to the 5th century; Rinaldo da Concorreggio was archbishop of Ravenna (died 1321).
It stands in the Chapel of the Madonna del Sudore in the cathedral.
cur:catacombs-ravenna-rinaldo-sarcophagu.notes: The apostles' identification as Peter and Paul is the usual reading.

cur:manuscripts2-menologion-baptism.summary: Christ stands in the river Jordan as John, on the bank, lays his hand on his head; a ray descends from heaven above him, and angels wait on the opposite bank to receive him. The miniature marks the feast of the Theophany on 6 January.
facts: The Menologion of Basil II, made at Constantinople for Emperor Basil II (976–1025), holds about 430 miniatures by eight painters whose names — among them Pantoleon, Michael of Blachernai and Nestor — are written beside each image.
It covers only the first half of the church year, September to February, and passed through the hands of Ludovico Sforza, Duke of Milan, before Pope Paul V received it for the Vatican Library.
cur:manuscripts2-menologion-baptism.notes: Page 299 according to the Commons description.

cur:monumental-san-paralytic-capernaum.summary: At the right, two men on the opened tiled roof of a house lower a paralysed man on his bed by ropes; at the left Christ, haloed and in purple, turns towards him with a disciple at his side. The panel shows with charming directness the faith of the friends who broke open a roof to bring the sick man before Jesus.
facts: The thirteen scenes of the north wall show Christ's miracles and teaching; in all of them he appears young and beardless, robed in imperial purple.
The scenes were not arranged in biblical order but are thought to follow the Gospel readings of the Lenten liturgy in Theodoric's palace church.

cur:objects3-clonmacnoise-south-cross.summary: The South Cross at Clonmacnoise is covered almost entirely with bosses, spirals and interlace, but at the top of the shaft on its west face a single Christian scene is set: Christ crucified, in a long robe, with the sponge-bearer and the spear-bearer at his sides. Now displayed indoors in the visitor centre, the cross shows how early Irish sculptors placed the Crucifixion at the heart of an otherwise abstract decoration.
facts: This is the only Christian figure scene on the cross; many believe the South Cross was a partial inspiration for the later and more elaborate Cross of the Scriptures at the same monastery.
The original was moved into the visitor centre to protect it from the weather, and a replica stands on its old site at the southern end of the monastery's central area.
cur:objects3-clonmacnoise-south-cross.notes: The figures flanking Christ are identified as Stephaton and Longinus from their poses and the conventions of Irish crosses.
